When the shrine doors open, the realm of the dead opens with them. According to Taoist belief, the wandering souls of those without proper burial will return to the mortal world during the entire seventh lunar month. The offerings placed on the altar at Lao Da Gong Temple are meant precisely for these unburied spirits. As snacks and refreshments dedicated to these forgotten souls — known in Taiwan as "good brothers" — gradually pile up on the altars, temple staff carry the tables out one by one, repeatedly clearing space; yet as worshippers come and go, the tables are filled up again, one after another.

Keelung City Councillor Chang Chih-hao, who was invited to attend the shrine-door-opening ceremony, remarked: "This is a very touching occasion. For our own departed family members, we would normally pay our respects at Qingming (Taiwan's tomb-sweeping festival). But Zhongyuan Pudu is different — it is directed at all beings between heaven and earth. Whether they can be seen in Taiwan or not, whether their names are known or not, we worship them all together."

The first day of the seventh lunar month marks the beginning of the Ghost Festival each year, known in Taiwan as Zhongyuan Festival. Within the Taoist faith, Ghost Festival rituals are observed by communities all around the world. In Taiwan, most Zhongyuan Festival observances are organised by individual neighbourhoods on the fifteenth day of the seventh lunar month, with some members of the public also visiting temples during the month to pray for peace. But in Keelung, as Du Feng-rui explained: "Keelung places particular emphasis on the Zhongyuan Festival — it is much like Keelung's own New Year." From the seventh lunar month until the first day of the eighth month, the city's fifteen surname-based clan associations, together with the municipal government, will jointly hold a series of ceremonies — including opening the shrine doors, releasing water lanterns, Pudu (that is, inviting the wandering spirits to a feast), the Dance of Zhong Kui, and closing the shrine doors — all in honour of the deceased.

Keelung's position as a strategically contested location has exposed it to numerous conflicts. From the Zhangzhou-Quanzhou clan wars and the Sino-French War through to the Second World War, when the city served as a Japanese naval base and was bombed by American aircraft, Keelung was also at the forefront of Taiwan's February 28 Incident. The Zhongyuan Festival held each year in Keelung has, alongside the city's own historical evolution, come to commemorate the deceased from across different communities.
